Aberdeen is a North Sea port city in Scotland located between the rivers Dee and Don. By population (around 230,000) the city is ranked the UK's 37th. The company Northlink Ferries provides regularly scheduled crossings connecting Aberdeen with the Northern Isles, Lerwick (Mainland Shetland) and Kirkwall (Orkney Island).

Founded as a fishing port on Dee River's estuary, Aberdeen Harbour (locode GBABD) has continually been improved. It is currently a major cargo port for export goods shipped from UK to Scandinavia (Baltic Sea in general). Major exports include granite, chemicals, fertilizers.

By cruise liners, the Port is usually visited on "Around Britain" itineraries, as well as on some Scandinavian (Baltic Sea) itineraries. Port's cruising season is early-May through early-September. Harbour's water depth (max draft) is 10,5 m (35 ft).

In 2017, the cruise port handled 25 ship calls and 2095 passengers. In 2018, at Aberdeen Harbour were handled 27 cruise ship calls and 3387 passengers (61% increase over 2017). In 2018, NorthLink ferry traffic increased by 5% (to 151,000+ passengers). The total number of ship calls increased from 6775 (2017) to 9266 (2018). The Port's total ship tonnage increased 5%.

In 2018 were continued the works on the harbor's north breakwater - part of GBP 350 million port expansion project at Nigg Bay (completed in 2020). The Harbour's expansion allowed docking of larger passenger ships, also ranking Port Aberdeen as Scotland's largest by berth capacity.

On May 29, 2019, Aberdeen Harbour welcomed its ever-longest vessel - the 175-m/574-ft MV Beltnes (IMO 9432206). The Self Discharging Bulk Carrier arrived to discharge 35000 tons of Norway-quarried fill material at South Harbour (behind the concrete caissons). The operation was part of the GBP 350 million South Harbour construction project, and particularly for creating the two new quays (Dunnottar and Castlegate). Both docks are designed to support activities associated with the booming renewable energy industry.

In late September 2020, Aberdeen Harbour Board awarded Royal Van Oord (1868-founded Dutch company specializing in dredging, land reclamation, and artificial islands construction) with two contracts for Aberdeen South Harbour's expansion. The project included rock removal and revetment (coastal engineering/shore protection) works. South Harbour's expansion (budgeted ~GBP 400M) became the UK's largest marine infrastructure project and was completed in April 2023.

  • AIDAaura was the first to visit the expanded South Harbour (on May 1st).
  • South Harbour's official opening was scheduled for September 22nd, with the ceremony presided by Her Royal Highness Princess Royal (Princess Anne of Edinburgh, 1950-born as Anne Elizabeth Alice Louise).
  • Now, South Harbour comprises four quays (Balmoral, Castlegate, Dunnottar, Crathes) with a combined quayside length of 1 mi/1,5 km.

In 2023, cruise ships were handled at three quays, representing over 40% of Aberdeen's cruise calls.

A short, restriction-free channel provides straightforward harbor access (entry and egress/exiting) and allows vessels to quickly navigate the pilot buoy.

In November 2021, the Port received GBP 0,4 million (~EUR 0,48M) in Government funding for a demo "Feasibility Study for Shore Power" (via a partnership with Connected Places Catapult) for a shoreside power supply facility within North Harbour. The technology allows berthed ships to turn off their engines/diesel generators and instead use electricity from the port's/city's power grid.

In 2023 (May through October) the cruise port handled a total of 43 ship calls (~33000 tourists). For season 2024 were scheduled/booked 55 calls. Stats for 2023 showed that each cruise ship visit resulted in an average of GBP 134 (EUR 154/USD 163) per person in passenger expenditure.

In 2024, the Port had scheduled 60 cruise ship calls (+150% over 2022). In 2025 (April to September) were booked 63 ship berthings with estimated ~40,000 passengers.

Aberdeen is Scotland's oil industry center, university center, as well as one of the country's largest seaside resorts. Best-known tourist attractions include St Machar's Cathedral (15th-century), Mercat Cross (17th-century), Brig o' Balgownie (14th-century, Scotland's oldest bridge), and Winter Garden (Europe's largest indoor garden). Old Town Aberdeen is the "students' quarter", also housing the campuses of two 15th-century universities - King's College (est 1495) and Marischal College (est 1500) - now combined into the University of Aberdeen.

The city is perfect as a base for touring the nearby castles Crathes, Dunnotar, and Slains, as well as the whisky distilleries Glenlivet, Glenfiddich, Speyside Cooperage. Other popular sites include the Royal Family's summer residence Balmoral Castle, and the Braemar Castle, which hosts the Highland's largest games every September.

During the mid-18th-mid-20th centuries, the town's buildings incorporated locally quarried grey granite, that sparkles like silver due to its high mica content.

Aberdeen cruise terminal

In 2017, Port Aberdeen started building a new deepwater harbour to attract larger-sized cruise liners (with max capacity 5000 passengers and crew). The new facility is scheduled for completion in 2020.

Currently, Aberdeen is a tender cruise port and handles annually around 30 smaller-sized vessels. After the vessel anchors, its passengers are transported ashore via the ship's tender boats. The new / deeper harbor will allow direct (quayside) disembarkation.

Aberdeen is a practical cruise port for independent sightseeing, but the experience depends strongly on the ship's berth. Larger cruise ships normally use the expanded South Harbour, several kilometres from the city centre, while smaller vessels may use berths in the older North Harbour much closer to central Aberdeen. Ships normally dock alongside rather than tender.

At a Glance

  • Independent sightseeing: Easy independently once in the city centre; some transport is normally required from South Harbour.
  • Best short-call choice: Aberdeen Maritime Museum, historic city centre and granite architecture.
  • With more time: Old Aberdeen or Stonehaven and Dunnottar Castle.
  • For countryside: Crathes Castle and Royal Deeside are better by organized excursion or pre-arranged vehicle.
  • Walking: Central Aberdeen is compact and generally easy to explore on foot.

Getting from the Cruise Port

Port of Aberdeen has two principal harbour areas. South Harbour, completed in 2023, has deep-water berths capable of handling ships up to 300 m (984 ft) long and now receives many of the larger cruise vessels. Cruise ships have used berths including Balmoral Quay and Castlegate Quay.

South Harbour is roughly 4–5 km (2.5–3.1 mi) by road from the central Union Square area, depending on the berth and port exit used. Walking from these berths into central Aberdeen is not a good use of limited port time because the route passes through and around working harbour and industrial areas.

Transfers arranged by the cruise line may operate on individual calls, but passengers should check the ship's daily information rather than assume a shuttle is provided. Taxis or pre-arranged vehicles are another practical option, with the journey into central Aberdeen normally taking around 10–15 minutes in ordinary traffic.

Smaller ships can sometimes berth in North Harbour, where some quays are much closer to Union Square, the Maritime Museum and the city centre. If the ship is assigned a North Harbour berth, walking may be practical after passengers leave the controlled port area.

Union Square is a useful starting point for independent travel. Aberdeen railway station and bus station are together here, providing easy connections for trips to Stonehaven and other parts of Aberdeenshire.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

Aberdeen City Centre and Maritime Museum

Allow 2–4 hours. This is the simplest independent option and works well even on a relatively short call. Aberdeen Maritime Museum overlooks the old harbour and covers the city's shipbuilding, fishing and offshore-energy connections.

From the museum, continue on foot through the historic centre to Castlegate, Marischal College, Provost Skene's House, Aberdeen Art Gallery and Union Terrace Gardens. Most of these sights are within a compact central area, so very little transport is required once passengers reach Union Square.

Old Aberdeen

Allow about 3 hours. Old Aberdeen is approximately 4 km (2.5 mi) north of Union Square and has a very different character from the commercial city centre. Highlights include King's College, the University of Aberdeen's historic campus, St Machar's Cathedral and the Cruickshank Botanic Garden.

Take a local bus or taxi from the city centre rather than walking the entire distance. Between April and September, the seasonal Aberdeen Adventurer sightseeing bus also serves Old Aberdeen. Once there, the principal sights are close enough to explore on foot.

Stonehaven and Dunnottar Castle

Allow about 4–5 hours. This is one of the best independent excursions from Aberdeen when the ship has a comfortable port call. Trains from Aberdeen to Stonehaven average about 17 minutes, making rail considerably more practical than many cruise-port day trips.

Stonehaven station is around a 15-minute walk from the town and harbour. From the harbour, a scenic coastal path continues to Dunnottar Castle, approximately 2.6 km (1.6 mi) south of Stonehaven. The clifftop walk takes roughly 20–30 minutes in each direction.

Dunnottar itself is considerably more demanding than the approach suggests. Entry involves a long descent and climb, including more than 200 steps, and there are no lifts or ramps into the castle. Passengers with limited mobility can still reach the clifftop viewpoint without entering the ruins.

For a quicker visit, use a taxi between Stonehaven and the castle rather than walking the coastal path. Leave additional time for the train back to Aberdeen and the final transfer from Union Square to the ship.

Royal Deeside and Crathes Castle

Allow about 4–6 hours. Crathes Castle is approximately 26 km (16.2 mi) west of Aberdeen and combines a 16th-century tower house with gardens and woodland. Banchory and the surrounding River Dee countryside can be added on a longer call.

Organized excursion or pre-arranged transport is preferable. Regional buses run along Royal Deeside, but using several local connections consumes valuable port time. A coach excursion or private driver makes it much easier to visit a castle and countryside stops while retaining a sensible return margin.

Balmoral Castle is much farther west, near Ballater, and its public opening arrangements are seasonal and can change during the year. Cruise passengers should only plan a Balmoral visit after checking that the estate is open on the date of their call.

Self-Guided City Centre Walking Tour

Union Square to Aberdeen's Historic Centre

Distance: approximately 2.5 km (1.6 mi).
Pure walking time: about 35–45 minutes.
Recommended total time: 2–3 hours with stops.
Difficulty: Easy. Mostly paved city streets with some gentle gradients.

  1. Union Square: Start here after arriving from South Harbour, or use it as the reference point if walking from a nearby North Harbour berth.
  2. Aberdeen Maritime Museum: Walk to Shiprow for views over the historic harbour and, if time permits, visit the museum.
  3. Castlegate and Mercat Cross: Continue through the lower end of Union Street to one of the city's main historic public spaces.
  4. Marischal College: Walk north to the large granite Gothic building that is one of Aberdeen's most recognizable landmarks.
  5. Provost Skene's House: Visit Aberdeen's oldest surviving townhouse, immediately beside Marischal Square. Check the day's opening arrangements if planning to go inside.
  6. Aberdeen Art Gallery: Continue west through the city centre to the gallery and surrounding cultural district.
  7. Union Terrace Gardens: Finish with a walk through the landscaped gardens before following Union Street or Guild Street back toward Union Square.

Passengers returning to a South Harbour berth should allow additional time for the transfer from Union Square or the city centre back to the ship.

Coast and Wildlife

Torry Battery and Greyhope Bay

Allow about 2 hours. Torry Battery overlooks the entrance to Aberdeen Harbour and is one of the city's best locations for watching bottlenose dolphins. Dolphins are seen throughout the year, although sightings can never be guaranteed.

Greyhope Bay Centre provides a sheltered viewpoint and café at the battery. The area is geographically close to South Harbour but is best reached by taxi or pre-arranged transport rather than trying to find a pedestrian route through the working port.

This is a useful choice for passengers who prefer wildlife and coastal scenery to museums, and it can also be combined with central Aberdeen when the call is long enough.

Practical Tips

  • Check the exact berth before planning the day. South Harbour and North Harbour have very different walking and transport requirements.
  • Do not assume that a cruise shuttle will operate; arrangements vary between ships and individual calls.
  • For South Harbour, a transfer or taxi into the city is usually more practical than walking.
  • Aberdeen railway and bus stations are beside Union Square, making it an excellent base for independent trips.
  • For Dunnottar Castle, wear suitable footwear and be prepared for steep steps and exposed coastal conditions.
  • Aberdeen weather can change quickly even in summer. A waterproof outer layer is useful for city walks, castle visits and coastal excursions.
  • For longer trips into Royal Deeside, allow considerably more return time than for a city visit or Stonehaven excursion.
  • Plan to reach the port well before the ship's final boarding time, allowing extra time for traffic and any required transfer through the harbour.
